title: The quiet build-up: 4.e3 and 4.Bf4
intro:
White develops without touching the tension in the centre. These are the easiest positions in the course to play, and the two moves are not as alike as they look: against 4.e3 the bishop comes straight out, and against 4.Bf4 it should wait.

## Against 4.e3, the bishop goes out at once

4.e3 shuts White's own bishop on c1 in behind the pawn chain. That is White's business, and it means White has no quick way to punish 4...Bf5, so Black takes the free move. Everything after that is ordinary development: ...e6, ...Nbd7, a bishop to d6, castle.

## Against 4.Bf4, take the pawn instead

This is the one line in the course where ...Bf5 is not the move. With a bishop already on f4 supporting the advance, 4...Bf5 5.Qb3 Qb6 6.c5! clamps the queenside and Black has no comfortable break. Play 4...dxc4 instead, which is exactly what chapter 1 does, and bring the bishop out a move or two later once White has spent time recovering the pawn.

## The trick to know after 4.e3

5.cxd5 cxd5 6.Qb3 hits b7, which the bishop no longer guards, and d5 at the same time. The answer is 6...Qc7. It defends b7, and it puts the queen on the open file opposite a bishop that has never moved, so 7.Qxd5 loses a piece to 7...Qxc1+.

## The knight trip to h4, and what the h-file is for

After 5.Nc3 e6 White often plays 6.Nh4 to trade the bishop off. Let it happen, and recapture on g6 with the h-pawn. The rook on h8 then sits on an open file, and that is not decoration: if White ever castles short and plays a natural move like Qc2, ...Bxh2+ wins on the spot, because the king cannot take a bishop the rook is defending.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Playing ...e6 first out of habit against 4.e3, when nothing is stopping ...Bf5. Answering Qb3 with ...b6 or a retreat, when ...Qc7 solves everything and sets a trap. Recapturing on g6 with the f-pawn, which leaves a hole on e6 and gives up the file. And playing ...Bf5 against 4.Bf4 because it is the move everywhere else.

tree.note: The Slow Slav. White builds a small, safe position and shuts in the bishop on c1 to do it.

children.note: Out it goes, for free. White has no quick way to punish it, because the bishop on c1 is behind its own pawn.

mistakes.note: Solid, and it is the very move this repertoire is arranged to avoid. There is no reason to shut Black's bishop in as well.
Also good, and it pins the knight. From f5 the bishop watches e4, which is the square White eventually wants.
Fine too, and 5.Bxc4 gives White the free developing move that a4 lines make White work for.

children.note: Normal development, and the knight defends c4 so that the tension can stay a while longer.
Now the pawn goes to e6, behind the bishop rather than in front of it.

mistakes.note: Also fine and it usually transposes. ...e6 keeps the dark-squared bishop's options open.
6.Bxc4 gives White the centre and a developing move at once, and Black has no ...b5 to gain time with.

children.note: White spends two moves to trade the bishop, which is the standard plan against ...Bf5 in every line of this opening.
Step back one square and let the trade happen. The bishop has already done its job by making White spend the moves.

mistakes.note: 7.f3 asks the bishop to move again, and it goes back to g6 anyway a move down.
7.f3 sends the bishop back to a worse square than g6, and it has achieved nothing on the way.

children.note: White carries out the plan, spending two knight moves and giving up a knight for the bishop.
Take with the h-pawn. The rook on h8 gets an open file without moving, and the pawns stay healthy.

mistakes.note: It leaves a hole on e6, blocks the bishop on f8 from ever seeing the kingside, and gives up the h-file for nothing.

children.note: White develops and eyes the diagonal that the bishop trade opened up.
Develop towards the centre. The knight covers e5 and clears the back rank.

mistakes.note: Also natural, and it usually transposes. Knights before bishops is the safer habit here.

children.note: White castles and prepares to break with e4 at some point.
The bishop takes the best diagonal it has, aimed straight at h2 behind White's king.

mistakes.note: Solid and duller. On d6 the bishop holds e5 and points at h2, which is where this line can be decided.

children.note: A small move and a necessary one. It takes g4 from the knight and gives the king an escape square.
Connect the rooks and keep both castling options open while White commits first.
children.plan: Castle long and use the open h-file, or castle short and prepare ...e5. The doubled g-pawns are not a weakness while the centre stays closed.
children.name: The 4.e3 build-up, with 10.h3

mistakes.note: Fine, and it commits the king to the side where Black's own file attack would have been.

children.note: A natural developing move, and here it is the losing one: nothing is watching h2 and the king has no escape square.
The bishop cannot be taken. The rook on h8 defends h2 down the file that ...hxg6 opened, so 11.Kxh2 is not even legal.

mistakes.note: It passes up a winning move. With a rook already on the open file behind it, the bishop sacrifice on h2 is worth checking every single move.

children.note: Forced. The other three squares beside the king hold White's own pieces, and taking the bishop is not a legal move while the rook on h8 defends it.
Step away with discovered check from the rook. Black is a pawn up, the attack is still running and White's king has nowhere safe to go.
children.plan: Bring the knight to g4 and the queen to h4 or h5. Keep the bishop on the diagonal that ends on h2 and do not hurry: White cannot untangle.
children.name: 4.e3 and the h2 pawn

children.note: White offers the trade at once, hoping that the recapture improves the queen.
Take. Declining costs a move and the bishop has no better square than the one it would go to anyway.

mistakes.note: Keeping the bishop is reasonable, and 6.Bxg6 hxg6 happens next move on White's terms rather than Black's.
6.Bxf5 exf5 leaves Black with a pawn on f5 and no bishop, which is the wrong half of the trade.

children.note: The recapture puts the queen on an active square, which is what White was playing for.
Solid. With the light-squared bishop already off the board there is nothing left to shut in.
White castles and thinks about the e4 break.
Develop and cover e5 and c5, the two squares White would like a piece on.
The last minor piece comes out and adds a third attacker to d5.
Modest and correct. On d6 the bishop would run into e4 with tempo once the centre opens.

mistakes.note: Active, and 9.e4 dxe4 10.Nxe4 hits the bishop, so Black loses a move putting it somewhere else.

children.note: The break White has been building towards. The centre opens while White has the freer pieces.
Take. Leaving the tension lets White play e5 and gain space for nothing.
White recaptures with a piece and keeps a small lead in space.
Trade a pair off. Every trade helps the side with less space, which here is Black.
The queen takes back and sits in the middle of the board.
Hit the queen and develop at the same time, which is exactly the tempo Black needs.
children.plan: Castle, then play ...c5 to trade the last central pawn off. With the light-squared bishops gone, an equal endgame is a fine outcome.
children.name: 4.e3 and the 5.Bd3 trade

mistakes.note: Safe, and it lets White keep the queen in the centre for another move. Gaining the tempo first is better.

children.note: White releases the tension and follows with Qb3, which is the one real try against an early ...Bf5.
Take with the c-pawn. It keeps a pawn on d5 and opens the c-file for a rook.

mistakes.note: 6.e4 hits the knight and takes the whole centre with tempo.

children.note: The point. The queen hits b7, which the bishop stopped guarding, and d5 at the same time.
Defend b7 and take the open file. The bishop on c1 has never moved, so 7.Qxd5 loses a piece to 7...Qxc1+.

mistakes.note: Offering the trade is solid, and 7.Qxb6 axb6 leaves Black with doubled pawns and White a shade more comfortable.
It defends b7 with a pawn and leaves c6 and a6 to White's pieces. The queen defends the same pawn and develops.
It holds the position and undoes two moves. There is no need to retreat when a developing move solves everything.

children.note: White develops with check before Black can finish the queenside.
Block with the knight, which develops and puts a second defender on d5.

mistakes.note: Also a block, and the knight has less to do on d7 than on c6 in this structure.

children.note: White castles and keeps the pin on the knight.
Solid, with the bishop long since outside the chain.
White finally moves the bishop off the square Black's queen has been eyeing.
Develop and prepare to castle. Black has no weaknesses and a rook heading for the c-file.
children.plan: Castle, then play ...a6 to question the bishop on b5 and put a rook on c8. The pawn on d5 is solid and the file is Black's to use.
children.name: 4.e3 and the 5.cxd5 trade

mistakes.note: Also useful, and it invites 10.Bxc6+ bxc6, which hands White a target on c6. Castle first.

children.note: White steps the bishop out of the queen's line before doing anything else, which is the sensible answer.
Take b5 away from the bishop and the knight, and prepare ...Nc6 without a check landing in the middle of it.
White develops and puts a third piece near d5.
Finish the pawn structure. Black is solid, with the better bishop and the open file.
children.plan: Play ...Nc6, ...Be7 and castle, then double on the c-file. The queen on c7 is already the first piece on it.
children.name: 5.cxd5 with 7.Bd2

mistakes.note: 9.Nxd5! Nxd5 10.Qxd5 wins a pawn: with the queen on c7 rather than d8, the pawn on d5 has one defender against two attackers. ...e6 fixes that first.

children.note: White develops and leaves the bishop on c1 where it is, which Black should notice.
Solid, and the trap stays set: the bishop on c1 is still facing a queen down an open file.
children.plan: Develop with ...Nc6, ...Be7 and ...O-O, then put a rook on c8. Keep watching c1: any queen move that leaves it undefended runs into a check on that square.
children.name: 5.cxd5 with 7.Nc3

mistakes.note: The knight is defended by the pawn on b2, so this is simply a queen for a knight.

tree.note: White gets the bishop out before e3. It is more ambitious than the Slow Slav, and it changes what Black should do.

children.note: Take, exactly as in chapter 1. With a bishop already on f4 the immediate ...Bf5 runs into Qb3 and c5, so the pawn is the better target.

mistakes.note: The natural move, and this is the one line where it is not the best: 5.Qb3 Qb6 6.c5! clamps the queenside and Black has no comfortable break.
Solid, and it shuts Black's bishop in while White's is already outside. That is the wrong way round.

children.note: White props up d4 and prepares to recover the pawn with the bishop.
Hold the pawn, as in chapter 1's 5.e3 line. Winning it back is going to cost White real time.

mistakes.note: It hands the pawn straight back after 6.Bxc4. Holding it costs White real time and Black risks nothing by doing so.

children.note: White develops and prepares a4, which is the only way to get at the pawn chain.
Open the path for the dark-squared bishop. The other one comes out to b7 later, along the diagonal ...b5 opened.
White castles and leaves the pawn for now.
Develop and get ready to castle. Black is a pawn up and every piece has a square.
children.plan: Castle, play ...a5 to hold the chain and ...Bb7 on the long diagonal, and give the pawn on c4 back for the open file when White finally attacks it.
children.name: The 4.Bf4 build-up

mistakes.note: The right idea in the wrong order. Get the king out of the middle before fixing the queenside.

children.note: White stops ...b5 first, exactly as in the main line, and worries about the pawn afterwards.
Make room for the bishop. The pawn on c4 cannot be held once a4 is in, so develop instead of clinging to it.

mistakes.note: Holding the pawn works here too, because there is no knight on c3 to make b3 bite. Giving it back and developing is simpler.

children.note: White develops and prepares to take the pawn back with the bishop.
Hit the bishop on f4 and blockade in the middle. A knight on d5 is worth more than the pawn on c4.

mistakes.note: Also natural. Hitting the bishop first asks a question White has to answer before recovering the pawn.

children.note: The bishop keeps the diagonal and takes aim at the squares behind the knight.
Offer the trade. With the dark-squared bishops off, the knight on d5 has nothing left to fear.
children.plan: Trade on g5 or e7, castle, then play ...b5 to hold the extra pawn or ...Nd7 and ...c5 to give it back for the centre.
children.name: 4.Bf4 and the 5.a4 clamp

mistakes.note: It kicks the bishop and weakens e6 with the king still in the middle. Developing does the same job safely.

children.note: White develops the knight first and keeps every recapture available.
Open the path for the bishop on f8 and get ready to give the pawn back on Black's terms.
White stops ...b5 before taking the pawn, and the position is now the 5.a4 line above by another order.
children.plan: Play ...Nd5, hitting the bishop on f4, then ...Be7 and castle. This is the same position the 5.a4 line reaches a move earlier.
children.name: 4.Bf4 and 5.Nc3
